Where it began

Salim Durani was born in Kabul on 11 December 1934, into a Pashtun family, which made him a rarity: an Indian Test cricketer born in Afghanistan. Cricket was the family trade. His father, Abdul Aziz Durani, played the game for a living, keeping wicket and batting for Nawanagar, and after impressing on a tour of Karachi he was offered work by the Jam Sahib. So when Salim was three the family left Kabul and made their home in Jamnagar. His father later coached a young Hanif Mohammad, which means the Durani household had a hand in the making of two Test cricketers.

The player

Durani was a left-handed batter and a slow left-arm bowler, and he played 29 Tests for India between 1960 and 1973. He made 1,202 runs at 25.04, including a hundred, 104 against West Indies in 1962, and seven fifties, and he took 75 wickets at 35.43, with three five-wicket innings and a best of 6 for 73.

His finest hour came in the 1961–62 series against England, which India won. He took eight wickets in the victory at Kolkata and ten more in the win at Chennai, and the series was largely his. Ten years on he was at it again, removing Clive Lloyd and Gary Sobers as India beat West Indies for the first time, at Port of Spain. In first-class cricket, for Gujarat, Rajasthan and Saurashtra, he made 8,545 runs with 14 hundreds.

What made him special

Above all he was a crowd's cricketer. He was famous for hitting sixes, and it was said more than once that he would hit one when the spectators asked for it. People called him a romantic, and they loved him for it: when he was left out of the Test at Kanpur in 1973, fans turned up with placards demanding he be picked.

The figures never quite caught the whole man. A single Test hundred in 50 innings is a modest return for someone so gifted, but those who watched him tended to remember the sixes rather than the averages.

Away from the middle

He was the first cricketer to receive the Arjuna Award, and in 2011 the Indian board gave him the C. K. Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award, its highest honour for a former player. He also tried the cinema, appearing in Ek Masoom in 1969 and in Charitra, alongside Parveen Babi, in 1973. In June 2018 he was a guest at the historic Test between India and Afghanistan, a match that brought together the country of his birth and the country he played for. He died in 2023, aged 88.

And finally

Hitting a six is hard enough when you choose the moment. Durani was said to hit them when the crowd chose it for him, which may be the most generous thing a cricketer can do for the people who have paid to watch.
